metadata.scope: e_anatolia (all baronies across k_anatolia and k_georgia)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_polybotus.first_mention_attestation: Bishop Strategius of Polybotus attended the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE); also listed in Hierocles' Synecdemus (6th century CE).
b_polybotus.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Πολύβοτος (Polýbotos), literally 'rich in pasture / feeding many cattle', referring to the wide grasslands of the Phrygian plateau near Bolvadin used for imperial stock-raising farms (metata).

b_germa_anatolia.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Roman colony (Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix Germenorum) by Augustus between 25 and 20 BCE.
b_germa_anatolia.etymology_analysis: Ancient Galatian/Phrygian toponym Γέρμα (Germa), cognate with Greek θέρμα ('hot springs') and Thracian-Phrygian *germo- ('warm'), later Romanized as Germokoloneia.

b_tyraion.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by Xenophon in Anabasis (1.2.14) during the 401 BCE march of Cyrus the Younger (written c. 370 BCE).

morphemes.translation: fortified town / place of towers (cf. τύρσις)

b_tyraion.etymology_analysis: Hellenized form Τυριάειον (Tyriaeion, also spelled Tyraion) of a pre-Greek Anatolian/Phrygian toponym, possibly related to Mediterranean/Anatolian *tursis ('tower, fortified settlement').

b_isaura.first_mention_attestation: Besieged by the Macedonian regent Perdiccas in 322 BCE (Diodorus Siculus 18.22).
b_isaura.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Ἴσαυρα (Isaura), the fortified capital of the Isaurians (probably a Luwian-speaking Anatolian people), later distinguished as Isaura Palaea ('Old Isaura') and Isaura Nea.

b_laranalia.first_mention_attestation: No historical attestation found for 'Laranalia'; appears to be a CK3/Paradox corrupted or invented barony name, likely garbled from Laranda (modern Karaman).
b_laranalia.etymology_analysis: Unattested in classical or medieval sources; almost certainly a Paradox/CK3 corruption of Laranda (Luwian/Greek Λάρανδα, modern Karaman) in Lycaonia/Isauria.

b_derbe.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by Cicero in Epistulae ad Familiares 13.73 (c. 46 BCE, referring to Antipater of Derbe); later in Strabo 12.6.3 and Acts of the Apostles 14:6.

morphemes.translation: narrow pass / gate (cf. Persian darband) or indigenous toponym

b_derbe.etymology_analysis: Greek Δέρβη (Derbē); often linked to Iranian/Persian darband ('barred gate, narrow mountain pass', reflected in Turkish Derbent) or a local Anatolian toponym.

b_barata.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 4th-century CE Tabula Peutingeriana (as Barata / Baratha) and in Late Roman/Byzantine itineraries and church lists.
b_barata.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Βάρατα / Βαράτη (Barata / Barate), an indigenous Lycaonian settlement name (sometimes spelled Barathra in itineraries by folk-etymological assimilation to Greek βάραθρον).

b_ikonion.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as Iconium by Xenophon in Anabasis (1.2.19) during the 401 BCE campaign of Cyrus the Younger (with Bronze Age Hittite precursor Ikkuwaniya).

morphemes.translation: Hellenized from Anatolian Ikkuwaniya; folk-etymologized as 'little image' (εἰκόνιον)

b_ikonion.etymology_analysis: Greek Ἰκόνιον (Ikónion), Latin Iconium, adapted from the Bronze Age Anatolian/Hittite name Ikkuwaniya (folk-etymologized in Greek from εἰκών/εἰκόνιον, 'image', via the Perseus/Gorgon legend).

b_lystra.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Roman colony (Colonia Iulia Felix Gemina Lustra) under Augustus in 6 BCE along the Via Sebaste; later visited by Paul in Acts 14:6.
b_lystra.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Λύστρα (Lýstra), Latin Lustra/Lystra, an indigenous Lycaonian toponym of pre-Roman origin elevated to a Roman colonia under Augustus.

b_pappa.first_mention_attestation: Honored as Pappa-Tiberiopolis under Emperor Tiberius (14-37 CE); minted coins from Trajan's reign and mentioned by Ptolemy (c. 150 CE) and Hierocles.

morphemes.translation: indigenous Pisidian toponym (possibly from Lallwort/kinship or local root)

b_pappa.etymology_analysis: Pre-Roman Pisidian toponym Πάππα (Páppa), later combined with the imperial dynastic title Tiberiopolis (Τιβεριούπολις) under Tiberius.

b_katakekaumene.first_mention_attestation: Described by Strabo in Geography (12.8.19, 13.4.11, c. 7 BCE - 23 CE) as the volcanic district of Katakekaumene.

morphemes.translation: burnt (perf. pass. part. fem. of καίω 'burn')

b_katakekaumene.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Κατακεκαυμένη (Katakekauménē, 'the Burnt Land / Burnt Country'), a choronym referring to the black volcanic lava fields of Kula in Lydia (also used as an epithet for Laodicea Combusta / Katakekaumene in Lycaonia).

b_aezani.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Strabo's Geography (12.8.12, c. 7 BCE - 23 CE) among the cities of Phrygia Epictetus, with Hellenistic Pergamene/Bithynian history from the 2nd century BCE.

morphemes.translation: mythologically linked to Azan, son of Arcas

b_aezani.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Αἰζανοί (Aizanoí), Latinized as Aezani; an indigenous Phrygian settlement name folk-etymologized in Greek tradition from the mythical Arcadian/Phrygian ancestor Azan.

b_nakoleia.first_mention_attestation: Listed by Strabo in Geography (12.8.12, c. 7 BCE - 23 CE) as one of the six cities of Phrygia Epictetus.
b_nakoleia.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Νακώλεια / Νακόλεια (Nakóleia), Latinized as Nacolea/Nacolia, an indigenous Phrygian city name.

b_midaeum.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in 35 BCE as the place where Sextus Pompeius was captured by Marcus Antonius's generals; also listed by Strabo (12.8.12).
b_midaeum.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Μιδάειον (Midáeion), Latinized as Midaeum, meaning 'city/place of Midas', after an ancient Phrygian king.

b_docimium.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the late 4th century BCE (c. 302 BCE) by the Macedonian general Docimus (Dokimos); later described by Strabo (12.8.14).
b_docimium.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Δοκίμειον / Δοκίμια (Dokímeion / Dokímia), named after its late 4th-century BCE Macedonian founder Docimus.

b_synnada.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned by Livy (38.15) as visited by consul Gnaeus Manlius Vulso during his Galatian campaign in 189 BCE.
b_synnada.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Σύνναδα (Sýnnada), an ancient Phrygian/Anatolian toponym (etymology uncertain; legendarily linked to Acamas and Macedonian colonists).

b_philomelium.first_mention_attestation: At least a Pergamene Hellenistic foundation; attested in Cicero's extant correspondence from 51 BCE (Ad Fam. 15.4) and later in Strabo.
b_philomelium.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Φιλομήλιον (Philomēlion), Latinized as Philomelium, a Hellenistic foundation named after a Macedonian/Pergamene founder Philomelos.

b_amorion.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the Hellenistic period; minted civic coinage from 133-27 BCE and attested in Strabo (12.8.13).

morphemes.translation: indigenous Phrygian toponym (possibly related to Aura/Amorra)

b_amorion.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Ἀμόριον (Amórion), Latinized as Amorium, an Anatolian/Phrygian toponym of pre-Roman origin (Arabic ʿAmmūriya).

b_antiochia.first_mention_attestation: Founded by the Seleucid king Antiochus I Soter (c. 281-261 BCE, around 270 BCE) as a military colony on the Pisidian-Phrygian border.
b_antiochia.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Ἀντιόχεια τῆς Πισιδίας (Antiócheia tēs Pisidías), named after Antiochus (father of Seleucus I Nicator or Antiochus I Soter) in the 3rd century BCE.

b_neapolis.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by Pliny the Elder in Naturalis Historia (5.42, c. 77 CE) as a town of Roman Galatia/Pisidia.
b_neapolis.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Νεάπολις (Neápolis), literally 'New City', a common Hellenistic/Roman foundation name in Pisidia.

b_sozopolis.first_mention_attestation: Attested under the Christianized name Sozopolis by 381 CE (Council of Constantinople; earlier founded in the Seleucid period as Apollonia).
b_sozopolis.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Σωζόπολις (Sōzópolis, 'City of the Savior / Redemption'), a late antique Christian renaming of the Seleucid city of Apollonia in Pisidia.

historical_names.name: Apollonia
historical_names.source: Founded during the Seleucid period (3rd century BCE) as Apollonia (attested in Strabo 12.6.4 and Res Gestae).
historical_names.notes: Renamed Sozopolis in the 4th century CE under Christianization.

historical_names.name: Apollonias
historical_names.source: Founded during the Seleucid period (3rd century BCE) as Apollonia (attested in Strabo 12.6.4 and Res Gestae).
historical_names.notes: Renamed Sozopolis in the 4th century CE under Christianization.

b_salda.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 attestation found for 'Salda'; Salda is a modern Turkish village and crater lake (Salda Gölü) in Yeşilova, Burdur Province.

morphemes.translation: local toponym of Lake Salda and Salda village

b_salda.etymology_analysis: Modern Turkish village and lake name (Salda, Yeşilova, Burdur) of post-867 attestation; the nearby classical settlement on Lake Salda was Takina.

historical_names.name: Takina
historical_names.source: Epigraphic rescript of Emperor Caracalla (212-217 CE) and Roman-era inscriptions from Takina on Lake Salda.
historical_names.notes: Salda is a post-867 Turkish toponym; Takina was the ancient Pisidian settlement on Lake Salda.

b_sagalassus.first_mention_attestation: Conquered by Alexander the Great in 333 BCE (Arrian, Anabasis 1.28).

morphemes.translation: indigenous Pisidian city name with Luwian -assos suffix

b_sagalassus.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Σαγαλασσός (Sagalassós), Latin Sagalassus; contains the characteristic Anatolian/Luwian toponymic suffix -(a)ssos.

b_parlais.first_mention_attestation: Established as a Roman colony (Colonia Iulia Augusta Parlais) under Augustus in the late 1st century BCE (c. 25 BCE) and attested by coins and Ptolemy (5.6.16).
b_parlais.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Πάρλαϊς (Párlaïs, Ptolemy: Παράλαϊς), a pre-Roman Pisidian settlement elevated to a Roman colonia under Augustus.

b_selge.first_mention_attestation: Sent ambassadors to Alexander the Great in 334-333 BCE (Arrian, Anabasis 1.28), with civic coinage dating back to the 5th-4th century BCE.
b_selge.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Σέλγη (Sélgē), an ancient Pisidian city (appearing on early epichoric coins as Estwediiys or similar local forms; etymology pre-Greek/Anatolian).

b_adada.first_mention_attestation: Attested in a 2nd-century BCE inscription recording a treaty of friendship and alliance with Termessos, and in Artemidorus of Ephesus (c. 100 BCE, quoted by Strabo).
b_adada.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Ἄδαδα (Adada), an indigenous Pisidian toponym of pre-Hellenistic Anatolian origin.

b_kaklouma.first_mention_attestation: Catalogued in the Barrington Atlas of the Greek and Roman World (Map 65, Lycia-Pisidia, grid G3) as a Roman-period settlement ('R', c. 30 BCE - 300 CE) near Tityassos (Bean 1970, 22).
b_kaklouma.etymology_analysis: Roman-era Pisidian toponym recorded in the Barrington Atlas (Map 65, *Kaklouma, tentatively located at Dalayman near Tityassos); indigenous Anatolian origin.

b_ouasada.first_mention_attestation: Bishop Theodorus of Vasada attended the First Council of Nicaea in 325 CE.
b_ouasada.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Οὐάσαδα (Ouásada), Latinized as Vasada, an indigenous Lycaonian/Isaurian city name.

b_mistea.first_mention_attestation: Inhabited in Hellenistic, Roman, and Byzantine times; known as Claudiocaesarea under Emperor Claudius (41-54 CE) and attested in Tabula Peutingeriana and Council of Chalcedon (451 CE).
b_mistea.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Μισθία (Misthía / Mistea), an indigenous Anatolian toponym near Lake Beyşehir, also styled Claudiocaesarea in the 1st century CE.

b_tyana.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by Xenophon (Anabasis 1.2.20, 401 BCE campaign) as Dana/Tyana; preceded by Iron Age Neo-Hittite Tuwana and Bronze Age Hittite Tūwanuwa (2nd millennium BCE).

morphemes.translation: indigenous Anatolian Bronze Age city name

b_tyana.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Τύανα (Týana), derived from Iron Age Luwian Tuwana and Bronze Age Hittite Tūwanuwa.

historical_names.name: Tuwana
historical_names.source: Bronze Age Hittite records (Tūwanuwa, 2nd millennium BCE) and Iron Age Neo-Hittite/Luwian inscriptions (Tuwana).
historical_names.notes: Continuity from Hittite Tūwanuwa and Luwian Tuwana to classical Tyana.

historical_names.name: Tūwanuwa
historical_names.source: Bronze Age Hittite records (Tūwanuwa, 2nd millennium BCE) and Iron Age Neo-Hittite/Luwian inscriptions (Tuwana).
historical_names.notes: Continuity from Hittite Tūwanuwa and Luwian Tuwana to classical Tyana.

b_comitanassus.first_mention_attestation: Appears in the 4th-century CE Tabula Peutingeriana under the name Comitanasso, 20 Roman miles from Perta.

morphemes.translation: indigenous Cappadocian/Lycaonian toponym with Anatolian -assos suffix

b_comitanassus.etymology_analysis: From Greek Κομιτανασσός (Komitanassós), Latin Comitanassus, an Anatolian settlement name exhibiting the characteristic -assos toponymic suffix.

b_garsaura.first_mention_attestation: Described by Strabo (Geography 12.2.6, 14.2.29, c. 7 BCE - 23 CE) as Garsaura, renamed Archelaïs by King Archelaus of Cappadocia (r. 36 BCE - 17 CE).
b_garsaura.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Cappadocian toponym Γαρσάουρα (Garsáoura / Garsaura), later renamed Archelaïs by Archelaus of Cappadocia and Colonia under Claudius.

b_nazianzus.first_mention_attestation: Seat of Bishop Gregory the Elder (c. 329 CE) and listed in the Jerusalem Itinerary (Itinerarium Burdigalense, 333 CE, as Nathiangus).
b_nazianzus.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Ναζιανζός (Nazianzós), also attested as Nandianulus; an indigenous Cappadocian toponym of pre-Roman Anatolian origin.

b_cybistra.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Cybistra in Cicero (Ad Fam. 15.2, 51 BCE) and Strabo (12.2.7); preceded by Bronze/Iron Age Ḫubišna (Shalmaneser III, 837 BCE).
b_cybistra.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Κύβιστρα (Kýbistra), Latin Cybistra, derived from the Bronze and Iron Age Anatolian name Ḫubišna / Ḫabušna.

historical_names.name: Ḫubišna
historical_names.source: Neo-Assyrian annals of Shalmaneser III (837 BCE) and earlier Old Assyrian/Hittite texts.
historical_names.notes: Classical Cybistra continues the earlier Anatolian city of Ḫubišna.

historical_names.name: Ḫabušna
historical_names.source: Neo-Assyrian annals of Shalmaneser III (837 BCE) and earlier Old Assyrian/Hittite texts.
historical_names.notes: Classical Cybistra continues the earlier Anatolian city of Ḫubišna.

b_parnassos.first_mention_attestation: Bishop Pancratius of Parnassus attended the Council of Serdica in 343 CE; also listed on the Roman road in the Antonine Itinerary (3rd century CE).
b_parnassos.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Παρνασσός (Parnassós), an Anatolian toponym with the Luwian -assos suffix (homonymous with Mount Parnassus in Greece, possibly from Luwian parna- 'house/temple').

b_aspona.first_mention_attestation: Documented in the 4th-century Roman itineraries (Itinerarium Burdigalense, 333 CE; Itinerarium Antonini) and represented by Bishop Catherius at the Council of Serdica (343 CE).
b_aspona.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Ἄσπονα / Ἄσπωνα (Áspona), a Late Roman and Byzantine city and road station in Galatia Prima.

b_kinna.first_mention_attestation: Bishop Gregorius of Cinna attended the First Council of Nicaea in 325 CE; preceded by Hittite Zallara.
b_kinna.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Κίννα (Kínna), Latinized as Cinna, a Galatian/Cappadocian town occupying the site of Hittite Zallara.

historical_names.name: Zallara
historical_names.source: Hittite period records (2nd millennium BCE).
historical_names.notes: Cinna was known as Zallara in the Hittite period.

b_charsianon.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 638 CE during the first wave of the Arab invasions of Anatolia as Charsianon kastron (Arabic Qalʿe-i Ḥarsanōs).
b_charsianon.etymology_analysis: From Byzantine Greek Χαρσιανόν (κάστρον) (Charsianón kástron), a major Cappadocian fortress and later Byzantine theme, traditionally derived from a personal name Charsios.

b_therma.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in Ptolemy's Geography (2nd century CE, c. 150 CE) as Saravena / Aquae Saravenae; Roman thermal bath built in the 2nd century CE and attested as Thermae Basilicae in Hierocles' Synecdemus (6th century CE).
b_therma.etymology_analysis: From Greek Θέρμαι Βασιλικαί / Latin Basilica Therma ('Imperial Thermal Baths'), referring to the 2nd-century Roman thermal spa complex in Cappadocia (modern Sarıkaya, Yozgat).

b_euaissa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 5th-century CE (400s) Byzantine ecclesiastical/geographical records as Euaissa / Euaíssós (Greek Εὔαισσα), tentatively located near Yoğunhisar.
b_euaissa.etymology_analysis: From Byzantine Greek Εὔαισσα (Euaissa), a Cappadocian town attested in late antique/Byzantine sources, likely of pre-Greek Anatolian origin.

b_galatia.first_mention_attestation: Recorded c. 180 BCE (Polybius 24.14) as the encampment of Eumenes II and Ariarathes IV against Pharnaces I of Pontus; later rebuilt and renamed Justinianopolis by Justinian I (527-565 CE).
b_galatia.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Μωκισσός (Mōkissós), Latin Mocissus/Mocisus, an indigenous Cappadocian toponym (with -ssos suffix), later elevated as Justinianopolis.

b_soanda.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by Strabo (Geographica 14.2.29 / p. 663, c. 20 AD) as Soanda/Soandos, and later in the Antonine Itinerary (p. 202) and Frontinus (Strategemata 3.2, as Suenda).
b_soanda.etymology_analysis: Soanda (Ancient Greek: Σόανδα, also Soandon / Suenda) is a Hellenized pre-Greek Anatolian/Cappadocian settlement name located near Uşaklı Höyük / Soğanlı in Cappadocia.

b_aspona_CHA.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman imperial road itineraries, starting with the Antonine Itinerary (§139, §204, c. 200 AD), the Tabula Peutingeriana (c. 300 AD), and the Itinerarium Burdigalense (333–334 AD), and as a bishopric at the Council of Serdica (343 AD).
b_aspona_CHA.etymology_analysis: Aspona (Ancient Greek: Ἄσπονα / Ἄσπωνα) is an ancient Galatian-Cappadocian city and road station on the Ancyra–Caesarea highway, corresponding to modern Sarıhüyük.

b_kaisereia.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Caesarea (Καισάρεια, Kaisareia) in honor of Emperor Augustus by King Archelaus of Cappadocia c. 12–9 BCE (earlier attested as Mazaca / Eusebeia in Strabo).

eponym.details: Named after Roman Emperor Augustus (Caesar Augustus) in the late 1st century BCE.

b_kaisereia.etymology_analysis: Kaisereia (Greek: Καισάρεια, Latin: Caesarea) means 'City of Caesar', bestowed by King Archelaus of Cappadocia c. 12–9 BCE on the ancient Cappadocian capital previously known as Mazaca and Eusebeia.

historical_names.name: Mazaca
historical_names.source: Strabo, Geographica 12.2.7 (recording Mazaca and Eusebeia)
historical_names.notes: Originally Mazaca (probably from Old Iranian for 'Mazdā-city') and Hellenistic Eusebeia before being renamed Caesarea c. 12–9 BCE.

historical_names.name: Eusebeia
historical_names.source: Strabo, Geographica 12.2.7 (recording Mazaca and Eusebeia)
historical_names.notes: Originally Mazaca (probably from Old Iranian for 'Mazdā-city') and Hellenistic Eusebeia before being renamed Caesarea c. 12–9 BCE.

b_herpha.first_mention_attestation: Attested by Strabo (Geographica 12.2.8, c. 20 AD) in his account of King Ariarathes damming the Carmalas River near Herpa (Ἧρπα).
b_herpha.etymology_analysis: Herpha (Ancient Greek: Ἧρπα, also Herpa/Erpha) is a Hellenized Anatolian toponym for an ancient Cappadocian town at a crossing of the Carmalas (Zamantı) River.

b_armaxa.first_mention_attestation: Attested as a road station in the Antonine Itinerary (§206, c. 200 AD) along the Caesarea–Satala route.
b_armaxa.etymology_analysis: Armaxa (also Armaza) is a Roman-era Cappadocian town and itinerary station near modern Gemerek, preserving an indigenous Anatolian toponym.

b_arasaxa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ptolemy's Geography (§5.7.8, c. 150 AD) as Arasaxa and in the Antonine Itinerary (§211, c. 200 AD) as Arassaxa.
b_arasaxa.etymology_analysis: Arasaxa (also Arassaxa / Arathia) is an ancient Cappadocian town and Roman road station east of Caesarea near modern Akmescit/Zerezek.

b_kyzistra.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ptolemy's Geography (§5.7.7, c. 150 AD) as Kyzistra (Κύζιστρα).
b_kyzistra.etymology_analysis: Kyzistra (Cyzistra, Ancient Greek: Κύζιστρα) is an ancient Cappadocian town near Zengibar Kalesi, bearing an indigenous Anatolian suffix (-stra/-istra).

b_zeila_CHA.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Zela (Ζῆλα) in accounts of the Battle of Zela (67 BCE) during the Third Mithridatic War (Plutarch, Life of Lucullus 35; Appian; later Julius Caesar's Battle of Zela in 47 BCE).
b_zeila_CHA.etymology_analysis: Zeila (classical Zela, Ancient Greek: Ζῆλα, modern Zile) was an ancient Pontic temple-city dedicated to Anaitis, attested from the 1st century BCE.

b_telmessos.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Greek Telmessos (Τελμησσός) in 5th-century BCE classical sources (Attic tribute lists and Herodotus); earlier attested in Hittite as Kuwalapašša (c. 1300 BCE) and Lycian as Telebehi.
b_telmessos.etymology_analysis: Telmessos (Τελμησσός) is the Greek adaptation of Lycian Telebehi and Hittite-Luwian Kuwalapašša, featuring the characteristic Anatolian -ssos suffix.

historical_names.name: Kuwalapašša
historical_names.source: Hittite Empire records (Kuwalapašša) and Lycian inscriptions (Telebehi)
historical_names.notes: Telmessos is the classical Greek form of the Bronze/Iron Age Lycian settlement Telebehi (Hittite Kuwalapašša).

historical_names.name: Telebehi
historical_names.source: Hittite Empire records (Kuwalapašša) and Lycian inscriptions (Telebehi)
historical_names.notes: Telmessos is the classical Greek form of the Bronze/Iron Age Lycian settlement Telebehi (Hittite Kuwalapašša).

b_cibyra.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned by Polybius (Histories 21.34) and Livy (History of Rome 38.14) in accounts of Gnaeus Manlius Vulso's campaign in 189 BCE.
b_cibyra.etymology_analysis: Cibyra (Ancient Greek: Κίβυρα, Cibyra Magna) is an indigenous Anatolian city name on the border of Caria, Lycia, and Pisidia near modern Gölhisar.

b_cridus.first_mention_attestation: Cridus is a medieval/cartographic spelling variant of Cnidus (Knidos, Κνίδος), a Dorian Hexapolis city attested by Herodotus (c. 440 BCE) and Thucydides.
b_cridus.etymology_analysis: Cridus is a corrupt Latinized/game-data rendering of Cnidus (Ancient Greek: Κνίδος, Knidos), the famous ancient Greek city on the Datça peninsula in Caria.

b_aphrodisias.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Hellenistic polis in the 2nd century BCE (c. 150 BCE) around an older Carian sanctuary of Aphrodite.

eponym.details: Named after the Greek goddess Aphrodite, whose cult image was housed in the city.

b_aphrodisias.etymology_analysis: Aphrodisias (Ancient Greek: Ἀφροδισιάς) means 'City of Aphrodite', named for the prominent cult of the Aphrodite of Aphrodisias in Caria.

b_cremna.first_mention_attestation: Attested by Strabo (Geographica 12.6.4–5, 12.7.2) in his account of its capture by Amyntas of Galatia (d. 25 BCE) and subsequent Roman colonization.
b_cremna.etymology_analysis: Cremna (Ancient Greek: Κρῆμνα) derives from Greek krēmnos ('cliff, precipice'), describing the fortified Pisidian city's defensive plateau above the Cestrus (Aksu) River.

b_attaleia.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 2nd century BCE (c. 200–150 BCE) by King Attalus II of Pergamon (r. 159–138 BCE).

eponym.details: Named after King Attalus II Philadelphus of Pergamon (r. 159–138 BCE).

b_attaleia.etymology_analysis: Attaleia (Ancient Greek: Ἀττάλεια, modern Antalya) means 'City of Attalus', named for its Pergamene founder King Attalus II.

b_phaselis.first_mention_attestation: Founded by Dorian colonists from Rhodes traditionally in 690 BCE, and attested in Herodotus (2.178) as an important Greek trading city in Lycia.
b_phaselis.etymology_analysis: Phaselis (Ancient Greek: Φασηλίς) is a pre-Greek Anatolian coastal toponym adopted by Rhodian colonists in the 7th century BCE.

b_limyra.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the Classical Lycian period (5th–4th century BCE) in Lycian inscriptions and coinage (as Zẽmuri) and Greek sources as Limyra (Λίμυρα).
b_limyra.etymology_analysis: Limyra (Ancient Greek: Λίμυρα) is the Greek rendering of the indigenous Lycian city name Zẽmuri, located on the Limyrus River in southern Lycia.

b_myra.first_mention_attestation: Ancient Lycian city Hellenized by the 3rd century BCE (c. 250 BCE) and attested in Strabo (Geographica 14.3.7) and the New Testament (Acts 27:5).
b_myra.etymology_analysis: Myra (Ancient Greek: Μύρα) is an indigenous Lycian city name associated with the river Myros (Demre Çay), Hellenized by the 3rd century BCE.

b_olbasa.first_mention_attestation: Established as the Roman colony Colonia Iulia Augusta Olbasa under Augustus (c. 25 BCE) and attested in Ptolemy's Geography (5.5) and Hierocles' Synecdemus (p. 680).
b_olbasa.etymology_analysis: Olbasa (Ancient Greek: Ὄλβασα) is an ancient Pisidian town near modern Belenli bearing a pre-Greek Anatolian/Pisidian toponym.

b_adrassos.first_mention_attestation: Ancient Isaurian/Rough Cilician town at Balabolu attested by Greek inscriptions and necropolis monuments dating from the 3rd to early 6th century AD, and as an Isaurian bishopric in late antiquity.
b_adrassos.etymology_analysis: Adrassos (Adrassus, Ancient Greek: Ἀδρασσός) is an ancient Isaurian/Cilician settlement name with the characteristic Luwian-Anatolian -assos suffix.

b_anemurium.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Roman/Greek geography (Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy) as Anemurium (Ἀνεμούριον) near Cape Anamur.
b_anemurium.etymology_analysis: Anemurium (Ancient Greek: Ἀνεμούριον, 'Windy Cape') derives from Greek anemos ('wind'), referring to the exposed southernmost cape of Asia Minor.

b_selinus.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 557 BCE as Sallune in the Neo-Babylonian Chronicle of King Neriglissar, and later in Pseudo-Scylax (4th century BCE) and Livy (33.20) as Selinus.

morphemes.translation: wild celery (σέλινον) / folk-etymologized local river-town name

b_selinus.etymology_analysis: Selinus (Ancient Greek: Σελινούς) was a port-town at the mouth of the Selinus river, attested in 557 BCE as Neo-Babylonian Sallunê and temporarily renamed Trajanopolis after Emperor Trajan's death there in 117 AD.

historical_names.name: Sallune
historical_names.source: Neo-Babylonian Chronicle of Neriglissar (557 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Attested as Sallune in 557 BCE prior to Greek/Roman Selinus (and Trajanopolis in 117 AD).

historical_names.name: Šalluna
historical_names.source: Neo-Babylonian Chronicle of Neriglissar (557 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Attested as Sallune in 557 BCE prior to Greek/Roman Selinus (and Trajanopolis in 117 AD).

b_korakesion.first_mention_attestation: Attested by Strabo (Geographica 14.5.2) as the stronghold used by Diodotus Tryphon c. 140 BCE and later captured by Pompey in 67 BCE.
b_korakesion.etymology_analysis: Korakesion (Latin: Coracesium, modern Alanya) derives from Luwian Korakassa meaning 'point/protruding city', describing its rocky Mediterranean promontory.

b_side.first_mention_attestation: Ancient Pamphylian city Hellenized after Alexander the Great's conquest in 333 BCE and attested in Arrian, Strabo, and local Sidetic coinage.
b_side.etymology_analysis: Side (Ancient Greek: Σίδη) means 'pomegranate' in the indigenous Sidetic/Anatolian-Greek tradition, an emblem that appears on the city's ancient coinage.

b_tarsus.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Hittite records of Kizzuwatna as Tarša (2nd millennium BCE, c. 1300 BCE) and later in Neo-Assyrian and classical Greek sources as Tarsos (Ταρσός).

morphemes.translation: indigenous Bronze Age city name in Kizzuwatna

b_tarsus.etymology_analysis: Tarsus (Hittite: Tarša, Greek: Ταρσός) is a Bronze Age Cilician/Kizzuwatnan city name preserved continuously through Assyrian, Persian, Hellenistic, Roman, and Byzantine periods.

b_adana.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Hittite inscription of Kava found at Hattusa as Adaniya under Kizzuwatna by 1335 BCE.

morphemes.translation: Bronze Age city stem (Adaniya), possibly related to PIE *danu ('river')

b_adana.etymology_analysis: Adana (Hittite: Adaniya, Greek: Ἄδανα) is attested since at least 1335 BCE in Hittite records of Kizzuwatna.

b_mallus.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 333 BCE when triremes from Mallus joined Alexander the Great's fleet (Quintus Curtius 3.7; Arrian; Strabo 14.5.17).
b_mallus.etymology_analysis: Mallus (Ancient Greek: Μαλλός, Latin: Mallus) was an ancient Greek-Cilician city near the mouth of the Pyramus (Ceyhan) River, traditionally linked to Mopsus and Amphilochus.

b_anazaribus.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Anazarbus by Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, c. 77 AD) and in 1st-century AD Roman/Cilician records (also home to Dioscorides).

morphemes.translation: local pre-Greek root (later folk-etymologized in Arabic as 'Ain Zarba)

b_anazaribus.etymology_analysis: Anazaribus is a variant of Anazarbus (Ancient Greek: Ἀναζαρβός), the capital of Late Roman Cilicia Secunda, later known as Justinopolis and Arabic 'Ain Zarba.

b_faustinopolis.first_mention_attestation: Established as a Roman colony in 176 AD by Emperor Marcus Aurelius at the Cappadocian village of Halala following the death of his wife Faustina the Younger.

eponym.details: Named after Roman Empress Faustina the Younger (d. 175/176 AD), wife of Marcus Aurelius.

b_faustinopolis.etymology_analysis: Faustionopolis is a minor spelling variant of Faustinopolis (Φαυστινόπολις), 'City of Faustina', elevated from the village of Halala in 176 AD.

historical_names.name: Halala
historical_names.source: Roman imperial histories (village where Faustina the Younger died in 175/176 AD)
historical_names.notes: Originally the Cappadocian village of Halala before being raised to Colonia Faustinopolis in 176 AD.

b_podandus.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Antonine Itinerary (c. 200 AD) and Itinerarium Burdigalense (333 AD), and later in Basil of Caesarea and Constantine Porphyrogenitus.
b_podandus.etymology_analysis: Podandus (Padyandus, Ancient Greek: Παδυανδός / Πόδανδος, modern Pozantı) is an ancient Cappadocian-Cilician pass town bearing the Anatolian -anda/-andos suffix.

b_lykandos.first_mention_attestation: First attested in early 10th-century Byzantine sources when the Armenian general Melias occupied and fortified the ruined site of Lykandos (c. 903–908 AD), which became a kleisoura and in 916 AD the Theme of Lykandos.
b_lykandos.etymology_analysis: Lykandos (Greek: Λυκανδός, Latin: Lycandus, Armenian: Djahan) is first attested in the early 10th century (c. 903–908 AD) as a Byzantine-Armenian frontier fortress and theme established by Melias.

b_comana_LYK.first_mention_attestation: Attested by Strabo (Geographica 12.2.3, c. 20 AD) and Pliny the Elder as Comana in Cappadocia/Cataonia (also linked tentatively to Hittite Kummanni).
b_comana_LYK.etymology_analysis: Comana (Ancient Greek: τὰ Κόμανα τῆς Καππαδοκίας) was a major temple-city of Cappadocia/Cataonia at modern Şarköy, likely continuing the Bronze Age name Kummanni.

b_arabissus.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Antonine Itinerary (§181, c. 200 AD) as a major road junction in Cataonia/Armenia Secunda, and as a bishopric at the First Council of Constantinople (381 AD).
b_arabissus.etymology_analysis: Arabissus (Ancient Greek: Ἀραβισσός, modern Afşin) is an indigenous Anatolian toponym with the -issos suffix, birthplace of Byzantine Emperor Maurice (539 AD).

b_cocussus.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Antonine Itinerary (c. 200 AD) as Cucusus/Cocussus, and famous as the place of exile of St. John Chrysostom (404–407 AD).
b_cocussus.etymology_analysis: Cocussus (Ancient Greek: Κουκουσός, Latin: Cucusus, modern Göksun) is an ancient Cataonian/Cappadocian town name of pre-Greek Anatolian origin.

b_seleukia.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the early 3rd century BCE (c. 295 BCE) by Seleucus I Nicator as Seleucia on the Calycadnus (Seleucia ad Calycadnum).

eponym.details: Named after Seleucus I Nicator (c. 358–281 BCE), founder of the Seleucid Empire.

b_seleukia.etymology_analysis: Seleucia (Ancient Greek: Σελεύκεια, modern Silifke) means 'City of Seleucus', founded by Seleucus I Nicator in Rough Cilicia.

b_corycus.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Roman campaigns against Cilician pirates (78–75 BCE) and described by Strabo (Geographica 14.5.5) and Pliny.

morphemes.translation: leather sack/wallet (κώρυκος) or Hellenized local Cilician root

b_corycus.etymology_analysis: Corycus (Ancient Greek: Κώρυκος, modern Kızkalesi) was an ancient port city in Rough Cilicia adjacent to the Corycian Cave.

b_claudiopolis_SELEUCIA.first_mention_attestation: Refounded/colonized as Colonia Iulia Felix Augusta Ninica Claudiopolis under Emperor Claudius (r. 41–54 AD) and attested in Pliny and Ptolemy.

eponym.details: Named after Roman Emperor Claudius (r. 41–54 AD).

b_claudiopolis_SELEUCIA.etymology_analysis: Claudiopolis (Ancient Greek: Κλαυδιόπολις, modern Mut) means 'City of Claudius', a Roman colony and Isaurian bishopric in the Calycadnus valley.

b_soloi.first_mention_attestation: Founded as an ancient Greek colony in Cilicia c. 700 BCE, and later refounded as Pompeiopolis by Pompey in 67 BCE.

morphemes.translation: local Cilician-Greek city stem (also source of the word 'solecism')

b_soloi.etymology_analysis: Soloi (Soli, Ancient Greek: Σόλοι) was a major Cilician port city founded c. 700 BCE, famous as the source of the Greek term soloikismos ('solecism').

b_tall_hamid.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 8th century AD by the Abbasids as the frontier fortress of Tall Hamdūn (تل حمدون, modern Toprakkale, Osmaniye).

eponym.details: Named after an early Abbasid-era figure Hamdūn (8th century AD, pre-867).

b_tall_hamid.etymology_analysis: Tall Hamid represents Arabic Tall Ḥamdūn ('Hill/Mound of Hamdun'), an 8th-century Abbasid fortress in Plain Cilicia later known in Armenian as T'il Hamdun and in Turkish as Toprakkale.

b_al-haruniya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 799 AD (183 AH) under Abbasid Caliph Harun al-Rashid as the frontier fortress of al-Hārūniyya (modern Düziçi).

eponym.details: Named after Abbasid Caliph Harun al-Rashid (r. 786–809 AD), pre-867.

b_al-haruniya.etymology_analysis: Al-Haruniya (Arabic: الهارونية, al-Hārūniyya) means 'The Harunian [Fortress]', founded in 799 AD during the reign of Abbasid Caliph Harun al-Rashid.

b_ayas.first_mention_attestation: The medieval name Ayas (Armenian: Այաս, Italian: Laiazzo) arose in the Middle Ages (post-867, prominent in the 12th–13th centuries under the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia) for the ancient Cilician port of Aegeae (Aigeai).
b_ayas.etymology_analysis: Ayas is the medieval Armenian and Turkish name (also Italian Laiazzo) derived from Ancient Greek Aigeai (Latin: Aegeae), the ancient Cilician port at modern Yumurtalık.

historical_names.name: Aegeae
historical_names.source: Hellenistic civic coinage (c. 120–83 BCE); Strabo, Geographica; Pausanias; Council of Nicaea (325 AD)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Greek Aigeai (Latin: Aegeae) was the continuous classical and early Byzantine name of the port prior to the medieval Armenian/Turkish form Ayas.

historical_names.name: Aigeai
historical_names.source: Hellenistic civic coinage (c. 120–83 BCE); Strabo, Geographica; Pausanias; Council of Nicaea (325 AD)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Greek Aigeai (Latin: Aegeae) was the continuous classical and early Byzantine name of the port prior to the medieval Armenian/Turkish form Ayas.

b_tskhumi.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Tskhumi (ცხუმი) in medieval Georgian sources from the 8th century (Duchy of Tskhumi established c. 786 under the Kingdom of Abkhazia); earlier classical settlements on the site were Greek Dioscurias (6th century BCE) and Roman Sebastopolis (1st century BCE/CE).
b_tskhumi.etymology_analysis: Derived from Georgian Tskhomi/Tskhumi (ცხომი/ცხუმი), generally linked to Svan tskhum ('hornbeam tree').

historical_names.name: Dioscurias
historical_names.source: Greek colonization of Colchis (6th century BCE) and Roman/Byzantine sources (1st century BCE/CE).
historical_names.notes: Known as Dioscurias in antiquity and Sebastopolis in the Roman/early Byzantine period before becoming Tskhumi.

historical_names.name: Sebastopolis
historical_names.source: Greek colonization of Colchis (6th century BCE) and Roman/Byzantine sources (1st century BCE/CE).
historical_names.notes: Known as Dioscurias in antiquity and Sebastopolis in the Roman/early Byzantine period before becoming Tskhumi.

b_nicopsia.first_mention_attestation: First appears as Nikopsis in the anonymous 5th-century periplus (identified with Palaia Lazike mentioned by Arrian in the 2nd century), and as Napsa (ნაფსაჲ) in the 8th-century Georgian Vita of Abo of Tiflis by Ioane Sabanisdze.

morphemes.translation: obscure; possibly linked to Adyghe Nygepsykho or Greek Nikopsis (Νικόψις)

b_nicopsia.etymology_analysis: Attested in Greek as Nikopsis (Νικόψις) and in Georgian as Nikopsia/Napsa; exact root etymology is uncertain, possibly connected to the Nechepsukho river.

historical_names.name: Palaia Lazike
historical_names.source: Arrian, Periplus of the Euxine Sea (2nd century CE) as Palaia Lazike; 8th-century Vita of Abo of Tiflis as Napsa.
historical_names.notes: Anonymous 5th-century periplus equates Nikopsis with Arrian's Palaia Lazike ('Old Lazica').

historical_names.name: Napsa
historical_names.source: Arrian, Periplus of the Euxine Sea (2nd century CE) as Palaia Lazike; 8th-century Vita of Abo of Tiflis as Napsa.
historical_names.notes: Anonymous 5th-century periplus equates Nikopsis with Arrian's Palaia Lazike ('Old Lazica').

b_bichvinta.first_mention_attestation: Founded by Greek colonists in the 5th century BCE and first mentioned in Strabo's Geography (1st century BCE/CE) as 'Great Pityunt' (Pityus).
b_bichvinta.etymology_analysis: Both Georgian Bichvinta and Russian/Greek Pitsunda/Pityus descend from Greek pitys ('pine tree'), referring to the pine groves on the cape.

historical_names.name: Pityus
historical_names.source: Greek colony (5th century BCE) and Strabo, Geography 11.2.14.
historical_names.notes: Classical Greek/Roman name Pityus (Pityunt) adapted into Georgian as Bichvinta.

historical_names.name: Great Pityunt
historical_names.source: Greek colony (5th century BCE) and Strabo, Geography 11.2.14.
historical_names.notes: Classical Greek/Roman name Pityus (Pityunt) adapted into Georgian as Bichvinta.

b_anacopia.first_mention_attestation: Prominent by the 8th century as capital of the Kingdom of Abkhazia; famously besieged by Umayyad commander Marwan II in 736–737 CE (recorded in Georgian chronicles; also mentioned in 7th-century Byzantine sources).
b_anacopia.etymology_analysis: Recorded in Georgian as Anakopia (ანაკოფია) and in Greek as Anakouphe; pre-867 fortress and capital of Abasgia/Abkhazia.

b_batumi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 4th century BCE by Aristotle as Bathus (Bathys Limen, 'deep harbor'), and later by Pliny the Elder in the 1st century CE.

morphemes.translation: deep (βαθύς, referring to the deep natural harbor)

b_batumi.etymology_analysis: Derived from Ancient Greek bathys ('deep', from Bathys Limen, 'deep harbor'), adapted into Georgian as Batumi.

historical_names.name: Bathus
historical_names.source: Aristotle (4th century BCE).
historical_names.notes: Classical Greek name Bathus / Bathys Limen.

historical_names.name: Bathys Limen
historical_names.source: Aristotle (4th century BCE).
historical_names.notes: Classical Greek name Bathus / Bathys Limen.

b_poti.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Milesian Greek colony of Phasis in the 7th–6th century BCE; the Georgian form Poti (ფოთი) enters written sources in the 8th century CE.

morphemes.translation: derived from the ancient name of the Rioni River (Phasis)

b_poti.etymology_analysis: Poti (ფოთი) derives from Ancient Greek Phasis (Φᾶσις), the classical name of both the Rioni River and the Milesian colony at its mouth.

historical_names.name: Phasis
historical_names.source: Milesian Greek colony founded 7th–6th century BCE; attested in Pseudo-Scylax and Strabo.
historical_names.notes: Ancient Phasis preceded the 8th-century Georgian attestation of Poti.

b_vartsikhe.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 6th-century Eastern Roman authors (including Procopius during the Lazic War, 542–562 CE) as Rhodopolis ('City of Roses'), corresponding to Georgian Vardtsikhe/Vartsikhe.
b_vartsikhe.etymology_analysis: Georgian Vard-tsikhe ('Rose Fortress') is a direct calque or parallel of its 6th-century Greek name Rhodopolis ('Rose City').

historical_names.name: Rhodopolis
historical_names.source: Procopius and 6th-century Byzantine sources (Lazic War).
historical_names.notes: Recorded in Greek as Rhodopolis in the 6th century.

historical_names.name: Vardtsikhe
historical_names.source: Procopius and 6th-century Byzantine sources (Lazic War).
historical_names.notes: Recorded in Greek as Rhodopolis in the 6th century.

b_shorapann.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 3rd century BCE as residence of the eristavi of Argveti; mentioned as Sarapana by Strabo (1st century BCE/CE) and Sarapanis by Procopius (6th century CE).
b_shorapann.etymology_analysis: Georgian Shorapani (შორაპანი), rendered in Classical Greek as Sarapana/Sarapanis; an ancient strategic fortress guarding the road between Colchis and Iberia.

historical_names.name: Sarapana
historical_names.source: Strabo, Geography (1st century BCE/CE) and Procopius (6th century CE).
historical_names.notes: Classical Greek rendering of Shorapani.

historical_names.name: Sarapanis
historical_names.source: Strabo, Geography (1st century BCE/CE) and Procopius (6th century CE).
historical_names.notes: Classical Greek rendering of Shorapani.

b_kutaisi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 3rd century BCE by Apollonius of Rhodes (Argonautica) as Aea/Cytaea, capital of Colchis (archaeologically settled since the 13th century BCE).

morphemes.translation: ancient Colchian root (cf. Greek Kytaia / Kotais)

b_kutaisi.etymology_analysis: From ancient Colchian *Kuta- / Greek Kytaia (Κυταία) and Kotais (Κόταις), modern Georgian Kutaisi (ქუთაისი).

historical_names.name: Aea
historical_names.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica (3rd century BCE).
historical_names.notes: Classical Greek names for Kutaisi.

historical_names.name: Cytaea
historical_names.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica (3rd century BCE).
historical_names.notes: Classical Greek names for Kutaisi.

historical_names.name: Kotais
historical_names.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica (3rd century BCE).
historical_names.notes: Classical Greek names for Kutaisi.

b_gudakva.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early Byzantine ecclesiastical lists (Notitiae Episcopatuum) and Georgian hagiographic scholia as Ziganis / Gudakva Eparchy (6th–8th century CE).

morphemes.translation: early medieval coastal bishopric and settlement

b_gudakva.etymology_analysis: Early medieval Georgian Gudakva (modern Gudava in Gali Municipality), identified with Byzantine Ziganis/Ziganeos in Georgian manuscript scholia.

historical_names.name: Ziganis
historical_names.source: Early Byzantine Notitiae Episcopatuum and Georgian scholion on the Martyrdom of St. Orentius.
historical_names.notes: Byzantine Greek name Ziganis identified with Gudakva (modern Gudava).

historical_names.name: Ziganeos
historical_names.source: Early Byzantine Notitiae Episcopatuum and Georgian scholion on the Martyrdom of St. Orentius.
historical_names.notes: Byzantine Greek name Ziganis identified with Gudakva (modern Gudava).

b_seti.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 written attestation for Seti (modern Mestia); the earliest surviving dated monuments in Upper Svaneti near Seti date from the late 9th to 13th centuries (e.g., 11th–13th c. churches and icons).
b_seti.etymology_analysis: Seti (სეტი) is the historical Svan name of the central community of Upper Svaneti, renamed Mestia in 1953/1968.

b_zugdidi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1572 (and 17th-century Georgian chronicles such as Beri Egnatashvili), becoming the capital of the Principality of Mingrelia (Odishi).
b_zugdidi.etymology_analysis: From Mingrelian zugu ('hill') + didi ('big'), meaning 'big hill', referring to the hill in the eastern part of the town.

b_tsageri.first_mention_attestation: Served as a medieval episcopal see of Lechkhumi (cathedral with portraits of Queen Tamar, r. 1184–1213; described by Vakhushti in the 18th century), with no specific pre-867 written attestation of the name Tsageri.

morphemes.translation: historical Lechkhumi town and bishopric name (ცაგერი)

b_tsageri.etymology_analysis: Georgian toponym Tsageri (ცაგერი), medieval ecclesiastical and administrative center of Lechkhumi.

b_kasriskari.first_mention_attestation: Part of the 5th–6th century CE northern frontier fortification line of Kartli (alongside Dariali and Khilaka) guarding the Kasri gorge on the Ardon River; later mentioned in Akhali Kartlis Tskhovreba and Vakhushti Batonishvili.

morphemes.translation: of Kasri (genitive of Kasri, gorge/area in Dvaleti)

b_kasriskari.etymology_analysis: Georgian Kasris-kari ('Gate of Kasri'), a fortified mountain pass blocking the Kasri gorge in historical Dvaleti.

b_ambrolauri.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical sources in the 17th century as one of the residences of the kings of Imereti.
b_ambrolauri.etymology_analysis: Georgian toponym Ambrolauri (ამბროლაური), first attested in the 17th century as a royal residence in Racha.

b_kvara.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical sources in the 11th century (Georgian Wikipedia: 'ისტორიულ წყაროებში პირველად მოხსენიებულია XI საუკუნეში').
b_kvara.etymology_analysis: Kvara (კვარა / კუარა), a high-medieval fortress near Skhvava in Racha.

b_zaqatala.first_mention_attestation: Established as a settlement/town in the 17th century (later fortified by Russia in the 1830s and granted city status in 1840); no pre-867 attestation for the town of Zaqatala.

morphemes.translation: uncertain; possibly linked to Sakas or local Avar/Tsakhur toponymy

b_zaqatala.etymology_analysis: Located on the Tala River in historical Hereti/Saingilo; the modern town name Zaqatala is attested from the 17th–19th centuries.

b_ghisi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Caucasian Albanian tradition (Movses Kaghankatvatsi) as Gis (Գիս), where St. Elishe (Elisaeus) built the first church in the 1st century CE; later a stronghold of Hereti (captured by David IV in 1117).

morphemes.translation: ancient settlement and church center (Georgian გიში, Azerbaijani Kiş)

b_ghisi.etymology_analysis: From Caucasian Albanian Gis (Armenian Գիս, Georgian Gishi/Ghisi გიში, Azerbaijani Kiş), an ancient religious center in Hereti.

historical_names.name: Gis
historical_names.source: Caucasian Albanian tradition recorded in Movses Kaghankatvatsi's History of the Country of Albania.
historical_names.notes: Gis is the earlier Caucasian Albanian/Armenian form corresponding to Georgian Gishi/Ghisi.

b_dedoplitskhara.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in medieval Georgian annals as a military post established by King David IV (r. 1089–1125); its name 'Queen's spring' is traditionally linked to Queen Tamar (r. 1184–1213).

eponym.details: Named 'Queen's spring' (Dedoplis-tsqaro) after Queen Tamar of Georgia (r. 1184–1213), who resided at nearby Khornabuji and piped water from the spring.

morphemes.translation: of the queen (genitive of დედოფალი, dedopali)

b_dedoplitskhara.etymology_analysis: Georgian Dedoplis-tsqaro ('Queen's spring'), named for the spring near Khornabuji associated with Queen Tamar.

b_nukhpata.first_mention_attestation: Nukhpata is a variant of Nukha (the name used for Shaki, Azerbaijan after the town was relocated near the village of Nukha in 1772 until 1968).
b_nukhpata.etymology_analysis: CK3/medievalized rendering of Nukha, the name borne by Shaki (Azerbaijan) from 1772 to 1968.

historical_names.name: Shaki
historical_names.source: Kingdom of Hereti / Shaki attested by 822 CE under Sahl Smbatean (and archaeological roots to 8th–7th c. BCE Saka settlement).
historical_names.notes: Original Shaki lay on the Kish River before being moved near the village of Nukha after the 1772 flood.

historical_names.name: Shakki
historical_names.source: Kingdom of Hereti / Shaki attested by 822 CE under Sahl Smbatean (and archaeological roots to 8th–7th c. BCE Saka settlement).
historical_names.notes: Original Shaki lay on the Kish River before being moved near the village of Nukha after the 1772 flood.

b_telavi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Teleda in the 2nd century CE by Claudius Ptolemy (Geographike Hyphegesis), and in Georgian manuscripts from the 9th–10th centuries.
b_telavi.etymology_analysis: Derived from Georgian tela ('elm tree'), attested in Ptolemy's 2nd-century Geography as Teleda.

historical_names.name: Teleda
historical_names.source: Claudius Ptolemy, Geographike Hyphegesis (2nd century CE).
historical_names.notes: Ptolemy's Teleda is identified with Telavi.

b_nektesi.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 2nd–1st centuries BCE by King Pharnajom of Iberia according to Georgian chronicles; a Christian church was built in the 4th century CE and the monastery established by St. Abibos of Nekresi in the 6th century CE.

morphemes.translation: ancient town and monastery name in Kakheti (ნეკრესი; input variant Nektesi)

b_nektesi.etymology_analysis: Georgian Nekresi (ნეკრესი; spelled Nektesi in the CK3 input), an ancient Iberian town and 6th-century monastic center in Kakheti.

b_mtskheta.first_mention_attestation: Capital of the Kingdom of Iberia from the 3rd century BCE to the 5th century CE, extensively recorded in the Georgian Chronicles and Classical sources.

eponym.details: Traditionally attributed in the Georgian Chronicles to the mythical eponymous founder Mtskhetos, son of Kartlos.

morphemes.translation: ancient capital of Iberia (მცხეთა), linked to ethnonym Meskhi or legendary Mtskhetos

b_mtskheta.etymology_analysis: Ancient Iberian capital Mtskheta (მცხეთა), traditionally derived from mythical Mtskhetos or the Meskhi tribe.

b_gavazi.first_mention_attestation: First documented in the 11th-century Georgian chronicle Matiane Kartlisa recording a 9th-century military victory by Bishop Samuel Donauri over Arab invaders at Gavazi (mid-9th c.); archaeological site includes a 4th–5th century tetraconch church.
b_gavazi.etymology_analysis: Georgian toponym Gavazi (გავაზი), site of an early Christian tetraconch church (4th–5th c.) and 9th-century battle recorded in Matiane Kartlisa.

b_kharnabuji.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Georgian sources in the 5th century CE, when King Vakhtang I Gorgasali built/fortified Khornabuji and founded an episcopal cathedral there.

morphemes.translation: sun (cf. Iranian khvar / xwar) or tribal name

b_kharnabuji.etymology_analysis: Georgian Khornabuji (ხორნაბუჯი; input Kharnabuji), often explained as an Old Iranian loanword meaning 'support/refuge of the sun'.

b_ujarma.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 3rd–4th centuries CE (attributed to King Aspagur I of Iberia) and expanded into a major royal residence by King Vakhtang I Gorgasali in the late 5th century.

morphemes.translation: early medieval fortress-town in Outer Kakheti (უჯარმა)

b_ujarma.etymology_analysis: Georgian Ujarma (უჯარმა), an early medieval fortress-town guarding the Iori River canyon since the 3rd–4th centuries CE.

b_lori.first_mention_attestation: Lori Berd (Lori Fortress) and its settlement were founded in the early 11th century (c. 1005–1020) by King David I Anhoghin of Tashir-Dzoraget.

morphemes.translation: fortress and province name (Armenian Լոռի, Georgian ლორე)

b_lori.etymology_analysis: Armenian Lori (Լոռի, Georgian Lore ლორე), founded in the early 11th century as the capital of the Kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget (Lori).

b_bolnisi.first_mention_attestation: Attested by the Bolnisi Sioni cathedral, built 478–493 CE, which preserves the oldest dated Georgian inscriptions (494 CE).

morphemes.translation: ancient settlement root in Kvemo Kartli

b_bolnisi.etymology_analysis: Georgian Bolnisi (ბოლნისი), an early Christian episcopal center in Kvemo Kartli attested by the 5th-century Bolnisi Sioni inscriptions.

b_kayan.first_mention_attestation: Built in 1233 CE by the abbot of Haghpat Monastery according to an inscription on the fortress church wall and Kirakos Gandzaketsi.
b_kayan.etymology_analysis: From Armenian kayan ('station/post/stronghold'), referring to the 13th-century fortress Kayan Berd near Haghpat.

b_tbilisi.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 5th century CE by King Vakhtang I Gorgasali (with earlier 4th-century fortifications), and made capital of Iberia by his son King Dachi in the early 6th century.

morphemes.translation: warm (თბილი / ტფილი, referring to the warm sulfur springs)

b_tbilisi.etymology_analysis: From Old Georgian Tpilisi ('warm place'), named after the area's natural warm sulfur springs.

historical_names.name: Tpilisi
historical_names.source: Georgian Chronicles (5th century CE).
historical_names.notes: Old Georgian spelling Tpilisi (ტფილისი) evolved into modern Tbilisi.

b_dmanisi.first_mention_attestation: Known among the six dioceses of Kartli in the 6th century CE, and mentioned in 853 CE when Bugha al-Kabir settled 100 Alan households there.

morphemes.translation: hamlet (Vakhushti derives Dmanisi from Old Georgian daba)

b_dmanisi.etymology_analysis: Georgian Dmanisi (დმანისი), explained by Prince Vakhushti as derived from Old Georgian daba ('a hamlet').

b_rustavi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early medieval Georgian sources (4th–5th centuries CE) as an important royal fortress-city and episcopal center of Kartli/Kakheti.
b_rustavi.etymology_analysis: From Georgian ru ('canal/stream') + tavi ('head/source'), referring to the headworks of an irrigation canal from the Kura River.

b_archabis.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 2nd century CE by Arrian in his Periplus of the Euxine Sea as Archabis (modern Arhavi, Turkey).
b_archabis.etymology_analysis: Greek Archabis (Ἀρχάβις), corresponding to Laz Arkabi (არქაბი) and modern Turkish Arhavi.

b_petra.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Novels of Emperor Justinian I in 535 CE, founded as a fortified Byzantine town in Lazica (modern Tsikhisdziri).

morphemes.translation: rock, crag (Πέτρα), referring to the rocky coastal promontory

b_petra.etymology_analysis: Greek Petra (Πέτρα, 'rock'), named by Justinian I's builders for the rocky promontory at Tsikhisdziri.

b_uplistsikhe.first_mention_attestation: Rock-cut settlement attested along the Kura River from at least the 5th century BCE (archaeologically inhabited from the 2nd millennium BCE; mentioned in Georgian annals from the 1st c. BCE / 7th c. CE).

eponym.details: Georgian written tradition attributes its foundation to the mythical Uplos, son of Mtskhetos.

morphemes.translation: of the lord (genitive of უფალი, upali)

b_tskhinvali.first_mention_attestation: First chronicled in Georgian sources in 1398 CE as a village in Kartli (under the form Krtskhinvali).
b_tskhinvali.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Georgian Krtskhinvali (ქრცხინვალი), meaning 'land of hornbeams'.

b_gori.first_mention_attestation: Town founded by King David IV of Georgia (r. 1089–1125); Gori Fortress first appears in 13th-century records (though the hilltop was fortified in antiquity).
b_gori.etymology_analysis: From Georgian gora (გორა, 'heap, hill, mountain'), referring to the prominent rocky hill on which Gori Fortress stands.

b_arthanuji.first_mention_attestation: Castle built by King Vakhtang I Gorgasali in the 5th century CE (Life of Vakhtang Gorgasali); besieged by Marwan II in 744 CE and restored by Ashot I Bagrationi as capital of Tao-Klarjeti in the early 9th century.
b_arthanuji.etymology_analysis: Georgian Artanuji (არტანუჯი; Turkish Ardanuç), derived from Laz/Armenian elements meaning 'edge of Ardahan/field'.

b_tmogvi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources during the Arab invasion of 914 CE (under Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj).
b_tmogvi.etymology_analysis: Georgian Tmogvi (თმოგვი; Armenian Tmkaberd), a clifftop fortress first attested in 914 CE.

b_akhaltsikhe.first_mention_attestation: The name Akhaltsikhe ('New Fortress') first appears in the late 12th / early 13th century (1204 CE) following reconstruction of the citadel under the House of Jaqeli; earlier known as Lomsia from the 9th century.
b_akhaltsikhe.etymology_analysis: Georgian Akhal-tsikhe (ახალციხე), literally 'New Fortress', replacing the earlier name Lomsia in the 12th century.

historical_names.name: Lomsia
historical_names.source: 9th-century fortress and settlement of Lomsia (Akhaltsikhe Castle / Lomsia Castle).
historical_names.notes: Before the 12th century, Akhaltsikhe was known as Lomsia.

b_artaani.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Artaani (არტაანი) under the Bagrationi princes of Tao-Klarjeti from the 8th–10th centuries CE (in the ancient region of Gogarene/Gugark mentioned by Strabo).

morphemes.translation: historical town and district name (არტაანი; Turkish Ardahan)

b_artaani.etymology_analysis: Georgian Artaani (არტაანი), from which Ottoman/Turkish Ardahan was borrowed.

b_tortomi.first_mention_attestation: Part of the historical Tao/Tayk region between the 9th and 16th centuries under the Kingdom of the Iberians and Kingdom of Georgia, with no explicit pre-867 written attestation for Tortomi itself.

morphemes.translation: town and valley name in Tao (Georgian თორთომი, Armenian Թորթում)

b_tortomi.etymology_analysis: Georgian Tortomi (თორთომი) / Armenian Tortum (Թորթում), modern Turkish Tortum.

b_taoskari.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Georgian settlement and fortress in Tao-Klarjeti (modern Çataksu, Olur), with medieval churches and Ottoman-era records (Taoskar/Tavusker), but no explicit pre-867 written attestation.
b_taoskari.etymology_analysis: Georgian Taoskari (ტაოსკარი), literally 'Gate of Tao', marking the boundary between Klarjeti and Tao.

b_oltisi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as a fortified settlement in the 9th century CE when the Georgian Bagratids occupied the region (with a 7th-century Greek-Armenian inscription reused in the castle).

morphemes.translation: ancient Tao/Tayk settlement root (Armenian Olti / Urartian Utu?)

b_oltisi.etymology_analysis: Georgian Oltisi (ოლთისი; Armenian Olti, Turkish Oltu), a fortified town in Tao.
